lessons.title: Structured Concurrency & CoroutineScope
lessons.content: Structured concurrency means every coroutine runs inside a scope, and a scope can't complete until all its children complete. This prevents leaked coroutines - if a ViewModel's viewModelScope is cancelled (e.g. the screen is destroyed), every coroutine launched in it is cancelled too, automatically. Real scenario: launching three parallel network calls inside viewModelScope - if the user navigates away mid-request, all three are cancelled without you writing any manual cleanup code.

lessons.title: Job vs SupervisorJob: Exception Propagation
lessons.content: With a regular Job, if one child coroutine throws, the parent scope cancels ALL sibling children too. With SupervisorJob, a failure in one child doesn't cancel the others. Real scenario: on a dashboard screen fetching 4 independent widgets (weather, news, stocks, calendar), you want one failing API call to show an error only in that widget - not tear down the other three. Use supervisorScope { } around the parallel launches instead of a plain coroutineScope.

lessons.title: CoroutineExceptionHandler & Cancellation Nuances
lessons.content: CoroutineExceptionHandler only catches exceptions from launch (not async - async defers the exception until you call .await()), and only at the top level of a coroutine hierarchy, not on every child. CancellationException is special: it's used internally to signal cancellation and should never be swallowed by a generic catch block, or you'll break structured cancellation silently. Real scenario: a common production bug is `catch (e: Exception) { log(e) }` inside a coroutine, which accidentally eats CancellationException and makes the coroutine un-cancellable - always rethrow CancellationException or check for it explicitly.
